title: What only the en banc may do
ask: Name what a Division of the Supreme Court cannot decide.
items: Cases on the constitutionality of a treaty, international or executive agreement, or law (Sec. 4(2))
Other cases the Rules of Court require to be heard en banc
Modifying or reversing a doctrine laid down en banc or in division (Sec. 4(3))
Dismissing a lower-court judge (Sec. 11)
A Division case that fails to get a majority of those who voted, and at least three

title: Qualifications of a Member of the Supreme Court
ask: List the qualifications of a Member of the Supreme Court and how one is appointed.
items: Natural-born citizen of the Philippines
At least forty years old
Fifteen years or more as a judge of a lower court or in law practice in the Philippines
Proven competence, integrity, probity and independence
Appointed by the President from a JBC list of at least three nominees
No CA confirmation; the vacancy filled within 90 days of its occurrence
src: Art. VIII, Secs. 4(1), 7 and 9; Kilosbayan; Sereno

title: What Kilosbayan v. Ermita held
ask: State the holdings of Kilosbayan Foundation v. Ermita (2007).
items: A Member of the Court must be natural-born
One who became Filipino through a parent’s naturalization as a minor is naturalized
BI and DOJ papers cannot amend a final naturalization ruling
A change in the civil register needs a Rule 108 court order
The appointee is enjoined until he proves natural-born status in an adversarial proceeding

title: No non-judicial work: the cases
ask: Give the rule against non-judicial work for judges and the three cases on it.
items: Sec. 12: no designation to any agency performing quasi-judicial or administrative functions
Meralco (1932): the Justices cannot be a board of arbitrators
Garcia v. Macaraig (1971): stop detailing judges to the DOJ; no executive may review a judge’s acts
Macalintal v. PET (2011): the PET is judicial work, so Sec. 12 is not violated

title: Guarantees of judicial independence in Article VIII
ask: List the guarantees of judicial independence in Article VIII.
items: Jurisdiction in Sec. 5 cannot be taken away by Congress (Sec. 2)
No reorganization that undermines security of tenure (Sec. 2)
Fiscal autonomy and automatic release (Sec. 3)
Appointment from JBC lists, without CA confirmation (Secs. 8–9)
Salary not decreased during continuance in office (Sec. 10)
Tenure during good behavior until 70 (Sec. 11)
Discipline of lower-court judges by the Supreme Court, not the executive (Sec. 11)
Exclusive rule-making power (Sec. 5(5))
Removal of Justices only by impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 2)

title: Removal: In re Gonzalez and Sereno
ask: What may and may not be filed against a sitting Justice?
items: Impeachment: the constitutional route
Quo warranto by the State on eligibility at appointment: allowed (Sereno)
Disbarment during incumbency: not allowed (In re Gonzalez)
A criminal charge carrying removal: not allowed during incumbency
Not an immunity: impeach first, then prosecute
The prosecutor dismisses such charges motu proprio
src: Art. XI, Sec. 2; In re Gonzalez (1988); Republic v. Sereno (2018)
hook: Impeach first, unless the title was never there.

title: The June 19, 2018 Sereno Resolution
ask: What did the Court hold in denying reconsideration in Republic v. Sereno?
items: Denied with finality, 8–6
Mere imputation of bias is no ground for inhibition
The six Justices’ House testimony did not disqualify them
Quo warranto by the State at its own instance is imprescriptible
Entry of judgment immediately
The JBC’s 90 days to fill the vacancy run from the Resolution
src: Republic v. Sereno, Resolution of June 19, 2018

title: Fiscal autonomy: what it bars
ask: What does the Judiciary’s fiscal autonomy forbid, and what does it allow?
items: No reduction below the previous year’s appropriation
No withholding or conditioning of release (Bengzon v. Drilon)
No outside body dictating how the Court uses or disposes of its resources (Re: COA Opinion)
No statutory exemption from court fees (Re: PHCCI)
Allowed: COA post-audit
hook: No cut, no hold, no outside hand.

title: RA 12233 (2025), the Judiciary Fiscal Autonomy Act
ask: List the main provisions of RA 12233.
items: The Court’s original budget proposal is attached to the NEP
The Chief Justice may augment Judiciary items from Judiciary savings
Allotments modified by en banc resolution
DBM releases one-twelfth monthly, without request or conditions
Quarterly reports to the President and Congress
COA post-audit of all Judiciary funds
A Judiciary Trust Fund replaces the JDF, administered by the Chief Justice
The Court sets legal fees, creates offices and positions, and takes title to its properties

title: Jurisdiction: limits on Congress and on the courts
ask: State the limits on Congress’s power over jurisdiction and the two jurisdiction cases.
items: Congress may define, prescribe and apportion jurisdiction (Sec. 2)
But not take away the Sec. 5 cases
No increase of the SC’s appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence (Art. VI, Sec. 30; Fabian)
Felipe v. Leuterio: no judicial power to reverse a contest’s judges; error is not a legal wrong
Almora v. Dela Rosa: in cases on the “application or operation” of regulations, the Court may order the government’s reports
src: Art. VIII, Secs. 2 and 5; Art. VI, Sec. 30

title: The Sec. 13 certification
ask: State the rules on the certification of consultation.
items: Conclusions are reached in consultation before the case is assigned for writing
The Chief Justice certifies it; the copy goes to the record and the parties
Members who took no part, dissented or abstained state why
A missing certification does not void the decision (Consing)
Not needed in administrative cases or per curiam decisions (Prudential)
Minute resolutions need no signatures or certification
Lower collegiate courts observe the same rules

title: Judicial privilege (In re Production, 2012)
ask: What does the judicial privilege cover, and what does it not?
items: Covered: the Court’s deliberations
Covered: predecisional records (raffle results, agenda, internal memos, drafts)
Not covered: external matters, such as bribery
Public records: produced as certified copies
The privilege belongs to the Court; no single Justice may waive it
src: In re Production of Court Records (2012)
hook: Public, yes; outside, yes; inside, never.

title: Votes in the Supreme Court
ask: How many votes does the Court need, en banc and in a Division, and what does a tie do?
items: En banc: a majority of the Members who actually took part and voted
Division: that majority and at least three
Division short of votes: the case goes to the en banc
En banc tie in an original action: petition dismissed (Rule 56, Sec. 7)
En banc tie on appeal: the judgment below stands
A tie lays down no doctrine (Cruz v. DENR)
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 4; Cruz v. DENR (2000)
hook: Count those who voted; a tie decides nothing.

title: Sec. 14: what passes and what fails
ask: Give the cases on what satisfies and what violates Art. VIII, Sec. 14.
items: Fails: testimony plus “credible” (Bugarin)
Fails: a labor tribunal with no findings (Miguel)
Fails: a one-page “no cogent reason” affirmance (Yao)
Passes: facts adopted from a party’s brief (Hernandez)
Outside it: a minute resolution refusing due course, with a legal basis (Nuñal)
Denials of reconsideration need only a legal basis (Martinez; Tichangco)
hook: Decisions: facts and law. Denials: a legal basis.

title: Memorandum decisions (Yao; Permskul)
ask: When is a memorandum decision valid?
items: It annexes the lower court’s findings of fact and conclusions of law
The annex is made an indispensable part of the decision
The decision adopted itself complies with Sec. 14
Only in simple cases: facts accepted, no doctrinal complication
Used sparingly, “lest it become an addictive excuse for judicial sloth”
src: BP 129, Sec. 40; Francisco v. Permskul (1989); Yao v. CA (2000)

title: Periods for deciding cases
ask: Give the periods for deciding cases, from submission.
items: Supreme Court: 24 months
Lower collegiate courts (the Court of Appeals): 12 months
Sandiganbayan: 3 months (PD 1606; Re: Delays), reconsideration in 30 days
Trial courts: 3 months (90 days), for cases, motions and incidents (Fuentes)
Submitted: on the last required pleading, brief or memorandum
After lapse: certification of the reason, and the court must still decide
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 15; Re: Delays (2001); OCA v. Fuentes III (2013)

title: The PET (Macalintal v. PET, 2011)
ask: State the holdings of Macalintal v. PET.
items: The PET is constitutional (Art. VII, Sec. 4, last par.)
The grant of “sole judge” power implies the means to exercise it
The Constitution “constitutionalized what was statutory” (the 1957 PET)
It exercises judicial power, “independent, but not separate” from the Court
So its Justices do not violate Sec. 12
Biraogo does not apply
src: Macalintal v. PET (2011); Marcos, Jr. v. Robredo (2021)
